hops.title: Why faint sounds vanish while loud ones still feel loud
hops.text: You might assume that if you need a louder signal to detect something, everyday sound must feel gentler. Inner-ear hearing loss often breaks that expectation. Healthy outer hair cells compress a wide range of sound levels into a smaller range of responses; when they are damaged, faint sounds are missed because the detection threshold rises, while the level at which sound becomes uncomfortable often sits about where it did before. The usable range narrows, and audiologists call this catch-up of perceived loudness as sound levels rise loudness recruitment. Someone who misses a quiet remark across the table can still wince when the speaker shouts.

hops.afterHeading: What this does and does not mean for people
hops.title: How a worn T-shirt changed mouse pain measurements
hops.text: A worn T-shirt left in a testing room was enough to skew pain experiments. In 2014 Robert Sorge, Jeffrey Mogil and colleagues found that mice and rats showed blunted pain responses when a male, but not a female, researcher was present. In mice, no person had to stay in the room at all: T-shirts worn by men, and certain compounds found in human underarm secretions, triggered stress and reduced pain-related behaviour. Before mapping a mouse behaviour straight onto human experience, it helps to remember that laundry can move the readout.

sources.citation: Sorge RE, Martin LJ, Isbester KA, et al., Mogil JS, Nat Methods 11(6):629-632 (2014)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A folded grey T-shirt sitting on a laboratory stool beside a clear enclosure with a curious mouse sniffing the air.
image.caption: In mice, men's worn T-shirts triggered stress that reduced pain behaviour: a readout is not an experience.

hops.afterHeading: Testing the peripheral target: the pharmacological control
hops.title: Why so little of an over-the-counter opioid reaches the brain
hops.text: The anti-diarrheal loperamide, sold over the counter as Imodium, is a synthetic opioid. In ordinary use, it calms the gut without morphine-like sedation, though drowsiness can occur. Little loperamide reaches the brain, largely because P-glycoprotein, a blood-brain barrier pump, sends it back toward the blood. In 1996 Schinkel and colleagues tested mice missing a gene for that pump: the ratio of drug-related radioactivity in brain to plasma was about seven times the control value, and in a separate test the antidiarrheal produced strong central opioid effects. Five years later Katrina Mealey and colleagues found ivermectin-sensitive collies missing the same four DNA letters from both copies of the canine gene.
